content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed 18 recommendations for the induction of labor at or beyond term. These recommendations are intended to be disseminated and implemented by all stakeholders involved in maternal care at international, national, and local levels. It is essential to enhance access to maternal healthcare services at the community level and to strengthen the capacity of healthcare facilities to provide high-quality care and information to all women during childbirth. These recommendations should be integrated into care packages and programs tailored to the specific needs of countries, healthcare facilities, and communities. Dissemination The recommendations will be distributed through WHO regional and country offices, advisory groups, ministries of health, professional organizations, collaborating centers, other United Nations agencies, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs). They will also be made available on the WHO website and shared during scientific conferences and meetings attended by WHO staff. The document will be translated into six United Nations languages, and technical assistance will be provided to regional offices for further translation and dissemination. Adaptation National and subnational groups may be established to adapt and implement these recommendations based on existing strategies. This process may involve revising national guidelines or protocols to align with the updated recommendations. Successful implementation of evidence-based policies requires well-planned, participatory, and consensus-driven processes. Ministries of health, United Nations agencies, professional societies, and other leadership groups often support these efforts. In humanitarian emergencies, adaptation should consider integration with other response strategies and address the unique needs, values, and preferences of women in such settings. Context-specific tools may be required to support implementation in these scenarios. Implementation Considerations The successful introduction of these recommendations into national programs and health services depends on participatory processes of adaptation and implementation. This may include revising national or local guidelines and protocols to meet the specific needs of each country and health service. Any modifications to the recommendations should be explicitly justified. An enabling environment should be created to support the use of evidence-based practices, including education and behavior change among skilled health personnel. Healthcare workers in antenatal care settings require training and supervision to perform dating ultrasounds. Additionally, health professionals need training to counsel women on the benefits and side effects of various labor induction methods. Women should be adequately informed and involved in shared decision-making regarding the indications and methods for labor induction. In lowand middle-income countries, health worker shortages may result in staff attending to a higher number of women in labor wards, potentially reducing their capacity to provide frequent monitoring or respond promptly to emergencies. Labor induction requires the availability of appropriate medicines, mechanical devices, monitoring equipment, and access to facilities for safe cesarean sections. Inconsistent supplies of medicines and equipment may pose challenges in some settings. Research Priorities The Guideline Development Group (GDG) identified several evidence gaps, including inconsistent data on the success of labor induction (defined as vaginal delivery rates after induction) across different settings and risk levels. Robust surveillance and the application of classification systems, such as Robson's classification, may improve data availability and consistency. The relative risks of adverse outcomes for mothers and infants associated with elective induction versus expectant management at various gestational ages and in different resource settings remain unclear. Ongoing and planned research may address some of these gaps, but further studies are needed to provide conclusive results. Monitoring and Evaluation The implementation and impact of these recommendations will be monitored at health service, country, and regional levels as part of broader efforts to improve maternal and newborn care quality. Data collection and evaluation at the country and regional levels will assess the impact of these recommendations on national policies. Local-level monitoring may involve clinical audits or interrupted time series analyses. Suggested indicators include the proportion of pregnant women receiving ultrasounds before 24 weeks of gestation and the proportion of women with documented indications for labor induction. Updating the Recommendations The WHO Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) reviews maternal and perinatal health recommendations annually to prioritize updates based on new evidence. If new evidence significantly impacts the current evidence base, the recommendations may be updated. Following publication and dissemination, any concerns about the validity of the recommendations will be promptly communicated to implementers, along with plans for updates. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to include in future updates. In summary, the WHO recommendations on labor induction aim to improve maternal and perinatal outcomes through evidence-based practices, tailored implementation strategies, and ongoing monitoring and evaluation.
